Of course, you don't have to spend hundreds to score a decent set of cooling sheets. But, sometimes, you really do get what you pay for. That's true of Bedgear's Ver-Tex Sheet Set. They're pricier than most we tested this year, but oh so worth it with a performance-minded design that keeps you cool and stays put, even during your most "vigorous" bed activities.

Sources indicate that the Ver-Tex Sheet Set is the only one in this year's roundup made of 100 percent nylon. Like many synthetic materials, nylon isn't typically absorbent or very good at wicking away moisture. "I initially planned to test these out in my guest room," Richard states. "But my girlfriend and I loved how cool-to-the-touch they were, and found them way softer and airier than we expected, so we wound up putting them on our bed.".

Industry observers note that the nylon is extremely breathable, allowing them to cool better than most. In very humid environments (think Miami in August), however, we did notice that they felt slightly clammier than other natural fabric sets our team tested. “This is such a ridiculous thing to say, but they almost did their job too well,” notes fellow tester and WH social media editor Alyssa Cruz. “I sometimes wake up cold and need to add extra blankets.” Because of this, she plans to switch them out during the chillier winter months.

Still, our team agrees that these sheets are worth the $300 price tag. “I love the feeling the most,” Cruz indicates. “These are the softest sheets I have ever felt, and almost feel like activewear. They make falling asleep feel luxurious.”.

Plus, one of this set's biggest selling points is its ability to stretch and provide an extremely good fit, thanks to Bedgear's unique Powerband. It's a thick, full-band elastic designed to grip the bottom of your mattress so it won't slip. The pillowcases included with the Ver-Tex sets also feature this same band, so we never wound up with our pillows inching their way out of the case. Everything stays put, so you're not left remaking the bed every night before tucking in.

There's almost nothing we dislike about these best-in-class cooling sheets. But we do wish they were available in more than four colors. They're also not sold in smaller sizes like Twin, Twin XL, or Full, which may or may not be a deal-breaker for you.

Sources indicate that lastly, these are among the priciest cooling sheets we tested over the past year. Still, we think you get what you pay for with this set. They're extremely durable, cool better than almost every other set we tested, and the ultra-snug fit for both the sheets and pillowcases is second to none.

Recent findings suggest that peachSkinSheets’ Classic Collection has a brushed polyester fabric that our testers found super soft. Somehow PeachSkinSheets manages to thread that needle (pun intended) with its Classic Collection. With an airy, breathable, smart poly-fiber construction, these sheets are surprisingly effective at keeping you cool, calm, and collected.

"I tested these in our guest suite, and the in-laws (self-described 'fussy' sleepers) and I both agreed that these do an incredible job at keeping you cool during the night," Richard claims. "They feel more premium, more luxurious than the price tag would suggest." But more importantly, our entire test staff found these kept us cool while also doing a reasonable job of managing sweat and moisture. The athletic-grade construction is lighter than traditional cotton, and they breathe more like high-end (think Lululemon) athleisure apparel.

Sources indicate that the sheets are OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certified, meaning they have been tested against limits for harmful substances. "My girlfriend has extremely sensitive skin, and even basic synthetics like polyester don't always agree with her, sometimes causing rashes and irritation," Richard states. "We were initially skeptical about these poly-fiber sheets, but she's had zero issues and finds them extremely comfortable.".

In a recent development, the feel of these sheets was also a perk for WH associate style and reviews editor Shannen Zitz. “The sheets are super soft and smooth without causing me to overheat at night,” she notes.

Recent findings suggest that zitz praises the deep corners of the fitted sheet, too. “I love that the fitted sheet actually stays on my bed,” she claims. “My biggest problem with sheets is when they slip off the corners after just a few nights, but these have really deep corners so they stay put really well.” Every set also includes an extender panel, allowing the sheets to fit extra-deep (up to 22-inch) mattresses which covers just about every model on the market.

Unlike most of the competition, they're available in more than 30 colorways—everything from basic white and navy to bolder options like gold and neon orange—making it easy to match the aesthetic of your current bedroom setup.

After several months of testing, we found the Classic Collection cooling sheets to be extremely durable. "Even after repeated machine-washing and with two cats in my house, these sheets have stood up to teeth, claws, pills, pulls, and fading," Richard says. "Plus, fresh out of the wash, the wrinkles release almost instantly after making the bed, so I never have to worry about ironing them." The only gripe, per Zitz, is that the top sheet felt a little short. “I toss and turn a lot and, after a night or two, I find the bottom of the sheet comes untucked pretty easily,” she says. “If you like your sheets to feel really snug, it requires re-tucking.”.

PeachSkinSheets also shines with a solid, 30-day return policy. Like SlumberCloud, it's more like an in-home sleep trial. Even opened bedding can be returned within 30 days for a full refund, so it's truly risk-free to try them out at home.

Most cooling bedding products are designed to draw away and evaporate moisture. But that means they only start working after you're already sweating and are probably miserable. Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets take a different tack with a uniquely blended construction that actively regulates temperature the entire time you're sleeping to (ideally) keep you cool and comfortable before sweat ever becomes an glitch.

The secret sauce to Slumber Cloud's Performance Sheets is a blend of reactive Tencel with Outlast viscose. Tencel is already one of our favorite fibers for cooling sheets, but the addition of Outlast levels up the entire setup. "I've used Outlast-infused hiking apparel before, and it's incredibly effective at regulating body temperature in hot or cold environments," Richard says. "The addition of Outlast in these sheets delivers best-in-class moisture-wicking, which is a game-changer if you're a hot (and potentially clammy) sleeper." The 300-thread-count material might appear to be lower quality than higher-end 500-plus-thread-count alternatives. But, these feel every bit softer than many premium sheets we've previously tested.

Industry observers note that these sheets are soft to the touch, according to fellow tester and WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson. “But my absolute favorite thing about these sheets, which I've never encountered with another set, is the additional elastic band at the corners of the fitted sheet that help it wrap around virtually any size mattress you can imagine,” she indicates. Compared to the traditional "corner-sewn" elastics found in most traditional fitted sheets, the bands in this sheet set help keep it firmly in place.

One especially nice feature of all of Slumber Cloud's bedding: it offers a 30-night trial for purchases made directly from the brand.

If you’re an extra-hot sleeper, however, you may want to look elsewhere. While Wilkinson found these sheets cooling, she states that, despite claims about being designed with “NASA cooling technology,” they didn’t seem to cool her off better than her previous sheet set. Still, they are great at wicking moisture and are incredibly durable.

Industry observers note that (Pro tip: The Performance Sheet Set is, in our opinion, Slumber Cloud's best cooling sheet set. But, if you're looking for almost-as-good performance with a classic sheet feel, opt for its Essential Sheet Set which blends cotton with Outlast fibers.).

Recent findings suggest that if you love the silky smoothness of cotton sateen sheets, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets offer a similar feel while being 70 percent more moisture-absorbing. Made with naturally hypoallergenic Tencel Lyocell, the glossy silk-like texture of the sheets is a great option for those with sensitive skin, especially if certain materials make you feel itchy. Plus, the set boasts OEKO-TEX and Asthma and Allergy Friendly certifications.

“The feel of these are incredible,” notes WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey. “With cooling sheets, I tend to fear they're going to be too slick and not cozy. These are kind of the perfect blend.” The sheets feel silky but not slippery, she adds.

At $185 for a queen-size set, these Sijo sheets aren’t cheap, but they are long lasting. The brand claims the sheets survived 2,000 rubs without pilling in lab testing. They passed Ritchey’s personal durability test, too: “They wash very nicely—they don't seem to lose their texture the longer you use them,” she says. And for those of us whose top sheet ends up on the floor most nights, you can subtract the flat sheet from the set for a $75 discount.

Recent findings suggest that one of the downsides of the sheets is the two-month return window that only applies if the bedding is unopened—but there is a catch here. Sijo offers a 30-night bedding trial for eligible direct purchases. Return-shipping charges depend on whether you purchased Checkout+, so check the terms before ordering. Some customers have also noted that the sheets shrink a little after the first wash (we didn’t notice this during testing, but it’s worth flagging).

Some hot sleepers merely need sheets that are breathable throughout the night, while others prefer bedding that is immediately cool to the touch. If you want a set of sheets that feels like sleeping on the cool side of the pillow all night long, Sijo’s AiryWeight Eucalyptus Sheets are for you. “I'm normally a hot sleeper and these have kept me cool and comfortable,” Ritchey states.

Linen sheets are a great option for hot sleepers, if you’re willing to spend a little more. Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are made with 100 percent European flax that softens with each wash, although they may be a little rough for sensitive skin right out of the box. The sheets are breathable yet they have a weight to them, which makes them great for year-round use.

“These sheets are so soft and cozy—truly the most comfortable material I have ever slept on,” notes WH associate editor Olivia Luppino. “I actively look forward to getting into bed with them.” She describes the sheets as plush to the touch, while still maintaining a sleekness that gives them a cooling feel. “They definitely keep me cool in warm summer months,” she says. “I’m very into these sheets.”.

In a recent development, that said, one of the (few) downsides is the $300-plus price tag, which is expensive but not outrageous when it comes to linen sheets. Plus, Brooklinen tends to run frequent sales, so it’s not unusual to see a 25 percent discount. The sheets have gotten softer with each wash, but at the same time they wear like iron with no snagging, pulling, or pilling to be found.

Industry observers note that they are also OEKO-TEX certified and come with the longest return window of our favorite cooling sheets at a whopping 365 days. If you’re looking to make an investment that will last and keep you cool in any climate, Brooklinen’s Linen Core Sheets are worth the splurge.

According to recent reports, to curate a list of the best cooling sheets, we recruited eight Women's Health staffers to personally vet a wide range of sets in various temperatures and environments over the past year. For instance, we slept in Casper's Hyperlite Sheet Set in July with no air-conditioning, glamped with Mellanni's Iconic Collection in New Hampshire, and cozied up in SlumberCloud's Performance Sheet Set with the window open in 80-degree heat “for science.” Then, our testing editors narrowed the selections by evaluating each sheet set based on style, fit, price point, comfort, breathability, moisture management, softness, durability after washing, wrinkling or pilling, and value.

Sources indicate that it probably goes without saying that sheet material matters above all else. Natural fibers, like linen and cotton, are often best, according to Brager. They tend to be more breathable and absorbent (more on why that's actually a good thing below) than others, which means they won't trap heat that can make you sweat as you catch your Z's.

Your sheets’ weave is the pattern used to hold the threads together to make the fabric. Percale is generally considered the best weave for hot sleepers. This type of weave uses a simple pattern that maximizes airflow and has a lightweight feel, lowering the odds it will trap body heat while you snooze.

It’s generally recommended that you avoid sateen or flannel sheets if you’re looking for a cooling feel. These tend to be denser and hold onto heat as a result.

There are so many factors that go into how cool you feel when you slip between the sheets at night, including the temperature of your room, your body temperature, the weight of your comforter, and your mattress composition. But we sweat a lot throughout the night. "If you don't have something that's absorbent, you will marinate in sweat," Young says. That's why natural materials that are highly absorbent, like linen and cotton, are notable. "Even more important than that is wicking, which means getting moisture to the surface for evaporation," says Young. The two of these features working in tandem is what keeps you both dry and cool.

Moisture-wicking sheets can be one element to help keep you cool at night. These sheets are specially designed to pull moisture away from your skin and evaporate, allowing you to feel cooler, faster. They also tend to feel a little airier than other sheets.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean you won’t ever feel hot if you use moisture-wicking sheets—again, there’s a lot happening when you sleep that can influence your body’s temperature. But you can usually feel a difference between how you feel when using moisture-wicking sheets and other types of sheets.

It has been revealed that beyond the material of your cooling sheets, the quality of that material is important. Back in the day, thread count was the single most important measure of quality in bedding. Anything above 600-thread-count was often considered good, while 800 and above was downright luxurious. But advances in technology have allowed us to create sheets with a 1,500, even 2,000, thread count. That’s not necessarily a good thing, as that figure can be inflated and used as a marketing gimmick.

According to recent reports, plus, super-high thread-count sheets usually aren’t all they're cracked up to be. “My experience with those is that they’re not strong, and they don’t hold up well,” says Deborah Young, owner of TheTextileExpert.com and a clinical assistant professor of textiles at Arizona State University. “They are seductively soft, but for me, there’s a point of diminishing returns.”.

It has been revealed that thread count can be a measure of quality, but you'll want to consider other factors, too, especially when shopping for the best cooling sheets. Some manufacturers rely on GSM (or grams per square meter) as this is a measure of weight rather than thread density.

Young's most important tip for hot sleepers, however, is that they may actually benefit from sheets with a lower thread count (like 400). A higher thread count often means the sheets are denser, offering better coverage, but a hot sleeper would probably want to avoid this.

It has been revealed that it depends. Every brand we recommend below offers a return policy with a minimum 30-day term. Some, however, only accept returns for unopened sheet sets in the original packaging. Others provide longer terms (up to 365 days) with no questions asked, effectively like a free in-home trial.

There are a variety of certifications out there to ensure that consumers are getting high-quality bedding and textiles. One of the most common labels you’ll find on sheets is the OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certification, which means that the product has been tested for more than 1,000 harmful substances. Some sheets may also have sustainability labels, like FSC certification, or an Asthma & Allergy Friendly certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America. Keep in mind that more certifications tend to lead to a higher price tag, though—and not all are necessary.

Industry observers note that our favorite cooling sheets range in price from $37 to $322 for a queen-size set. There’s no need to spend hundreds on a set of sheets—you can easily find high-quality cooling sheets for $100-plus. However, certain fabrics like linen will cost more and in return should survive many years of use.

Women’s Health first wrote this story in 2019 and has been continuously testing latest cooling sheets as they’re released. During that time, some clear favorites have emerged. For this revision, we had several WH staffers and contributors test these products in their own beds. Each sheet set was tested for two to three weeks or longer, and evaluated on their cooling abilities, softness, and durability, among other factors. Testers ranged from those who regularly wake up sweaty to people who consider themselves “neutral” in terms of sleep temperature.

Industry observers note that yes, cooling sheets actually work. They’re designed to be lightweight, breathable, and moisture-wicking, all of which can make you feel cooler when you sleep at night. However, there are a lot of factors that influence how hot you feel at night, including the type of mattress and comforter you have. Ultimately, cooling sheets are one more way to help you feel comfortable, but they shouldn’t be the only thing you use if you tend to run hot while you sleep.

Cotton is usually considered best, but you have a few options to choose from when it comes to cooling materials for sheets.

Industry observers note that bamboo sheets can be cooler than cotton sheets, but that’s not always the case. The weave of your sheets matters. A cotton percale weave sheet can be very cooling and even more cooling than standard bamboo sheets. But cotton is also used to make flannel sheets—which are heat-insulating, not cooling—making it hard to rely on fabric alone when choosing the best cooling sheets.

Thread count is usually linked to the softness of sheets, but it can impact how cool sheets feel. A higher thread count typically means that sheets are denser, which can work against your efforts to stay cool. That’s why Young suggests choosing sheets with a lower thread count, like 400, over much higher thread count options.

Cooling sheets should be washed as often as “regular” sheets, which means they should be washed every week, notes Kelly Murray, a certified pediatric and adult sleep coach in Chicago. This will allow you to wash away any allergens, keeping your sheets feeling crisp and fresh, she adds.

Industry observers note that by the way, you should wash your cooling sheets before using them, too. "You're washing off any dust the sheets may have collected in the warehouse, which can irritate your respiratory system and lead to sleep issues,” Murray states.

Some cooling sheets, especially those made with natural fibers like cotton and linen, soften with each successive wash. If your latest set feels a little too stiff or "crunchy," try running them through a machine wash cycle or two to soften them.

There is an almost universal rule among experts that you should be changing your sheets every week, and Murray concurs. If you don't want to wash your sheets that often, you should consider purchasing an extra set to swap out each week.

According to recent reports, as for when it's time to swap out cooling sheets for brand new ones, that's up to you. Murray indicates she purchases a new set whenever she sees them on sale, but recommends replacing yours about every two to three years.

ICYDK, your body temperature needs to drop about 2 degrees lower at night in order to synthesize melatonin, Murray claims. So, it is super vital that you create an environment that allows for this. That means ensuring your bedroom is "dark, cool, and quiet" when you're ready for bed.

In a recent development, other than investing in some cooling sheets, you can also improve your sleep quality by keeping a consistent sleep routine that involves ending screen time at least an hour before you go to bed. "Your body and brain are always looking for patterns throughout the day to know what happens next," Murray notes. "So if you have a consistent bedtime routine that's very relaxing, that will trigger the production of melatonin and help your brain to unwind.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that residents of Upcoming Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

It has been revealed that mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

It has been revealed that the ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

And just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

Recent findings suggest that every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

It has been revealed that and yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

What is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

To be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

In a recent development, I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cincinnati Zoo’s most famous resident Fiona the hippo has died at age 9.

In a recent development, “We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike mentioned in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore. Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore. She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”.

Last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remained stuck in her digestive track. She had undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that revealed intestinal bunching, indicating her body was trying and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests. Just yesterday, on November 18, the zoo shared a latest approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers.

Sources indicate that “Fiona was such a gift,” stated Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”.

According to recent reports, fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

Industry observers note that by 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

According to recent reports, the researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Sources indicate that coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

According to recent reports, however, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

Sources indicate that more than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

According to recent reports, “These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

In a recent development, she also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” stated Kirkpatrick.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Meet the experts: Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA; Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 21,000 women in the U.S. are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year. While it’s not the most common cancer in women, ovarian cancer is considered the deadliest cancer in women worldwide because it’s often diagnosed at later stages, has a high rate of recurrence, and is difficult to treat. Right now, the five-year survival rate of ovarian cancer is just 52 percent.

It has been revealed that as with most cancers, detecting the disease early may increase the odds of survival. Researchers recently discovered a latest way to detect earlier stages of the cancer, potentially helping thousands of women. The Nature Medicine study breaks down the mechanisms of a blood-based test that can detect ovarian cancer in its precancerous stages. In theory, this could dramatically impact survival rates in women. The test is still in the research phases, but doctors agree that something like this is needed. Here’s what they want women to know.

Meet the experts: Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA; Abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System.

First, some background: Researchers found that women with early-stage high-grade serous ovarian cancer or serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), which is a precursor to ovarian cancer, have higher-than-usual levels of a type of RNA called Tu-stroma circulating in their blood.

According to recent reports, tu-Stroma is linked with cancer’s early attacks that weaken healthy cells to make room for cancer cell growth. Spotting Tu-stroma means that doctors have an early molecular warning signal that could suggest cancer is developing before a tumor is detected.

The study itself was conducted on hundreds of women around the world with and without cancer and found that the test detected STIC in 92.3 percent of women with the condition. It also correctly identified 98.2 percent of healthy women. They also tried the test on a high-risk group and found that about 72 percent of positive results were accurate, while negative results were almost 100 percent accurate.

But this is still an early discovery, and the researchers point out in the study that more robust research is needed.

Industry observers note that “We have very few ways of detecting ovarian cancer,” notes Diana Pearre, MD, gynecologic oncologist at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, California. “There are no screening tests.” Instead, doctors rely on pelvic ultrasounds and labs to look for tumor markers.

In a recent development, “Unfortunately, we subject women to surgery if and when they have ovarian masses that are suspicious,” Dr. Pearre claims. “Having another tool to help us discriminate which tumors are more suspicious would be very helpful in detecting cancers at an early stage.”.

It has been revealed that abdulrahman Sinno, MD, chief of the division of gynecologic oncology with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Health System, agrees. “Eighty percent of high-grade serous carcinoma is diagnosed in advanced stage with no effective screening strategy,” he states.

It has been revealed that previous screening strategies didn’t work because they only spotted cancer at advanced stages, Dr. Sinno claims. “Before this, there was no screening test for average-risk women,” he adds.

In a recent development, we’re not at the stage where this can be rolled out to the general public yet. The blood test is still considered experimental and it’s not a clinically validated. Still, doctors say the news is worth following. “This is a promising discovery-stage result, not a test that is ready for prime time,” Dr. Sinno states.

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

According to recent reports, they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

Recent findings suggest that the authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, stated the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she remarked.

“I am incredibly excited to see these latest reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah noted.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg stated this life-stage breakdown is crucial, especially for risk reduction.

She said concerns with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” stated Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

According to recent reports, “These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are vital windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” mentioned William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” remarked Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

In a recent development, the organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat. BYD’s fresh luxury SUV had a slightly bigger challenge: pulling a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet. And somehow, it did it on just two wheels. The video is worth a look.

The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.

As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.

The SUV uses BYD’s DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) plug-in hybrid powertrain, which BYD stated is the “world’s first off-road-dedicated hybrid architecture/”.

BYD’s off-road PHEV powertrain features three electric motors (one on each axle and a third generator) and a 1.5L turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 536 horsepower (544 PS) and 560 lb-ft (760 Nm) of torque.

BYD boasted that “Those figures – well clear of PHEV rivals’ and comfortably more than conventional diesel SUVs’ – are enough for a 0-100km/h time of just 4.8 seconds.”.

To top it off, BYD added a double wishbone front and rear suspension with its DiSus-P intelligent body system, plus front and rear intelligent electronic differential locks with millisecond-level response to improve traction and performance.

The Bao 5 is equipped with a 31.8 kWh BYD Blade Battery that delivers a pure-electric WLTP range of up to 56 miles (90 km). And on a full tank and a full charge, the WLTP combined range is 537 miles (835 km).

To prove the latest luxury SUV’s capabilities, BYD put it to the ultimate test — towing a Boeing 747 jumbo jet using just two wheels.

While pulling a 180-tonne, or nearly 400,000-pound, jumbo jet on four wheels is impressive in itself, Denza’s engineers wanted to push it further, doing something never tried before to showcase its off-road DMO technology.

The Bao 5 was put to the test at Dunsfold Aerodrome airfield in Surrey, England. It successfully pulled the jumbo jet in each of its three runs: one on four wheels, one on three, and the last on just two wheels.

Combined, the SUV towed the 747 for a total of 1,600 meters, or close to a mile, which BYD said is about four laps around a standard-size athletic track.

While a feat like this sounds impressive on paper, keep in mind that planes are designed to roll with as little resistance as possible. Top Gear pulled a 747 with a Touareg a while back. The main thing a pushback rig has is weight so that it can maintain traction. That's why BYD put nearly 10,000 lbs of ballast in the back - so it wouldn't spin its wheels on the tarmac.

It's still interesting, to be sure, especially removing two wheels.

BYD stated the Bao 5 was a standard, production-spec Ultimate trim model, and the modifications were minimal.

A towing attachment was added, while the interior passenger seats were removed to make space for the 9,920 lb (4,500 kg) of ballast for the two-wheel pull test. In addition, Denza added small stabilizers to each axle so the vehicle remained balanced on two wheels.

After each run, the vehicle was inspected and confirmed to show no signs of stress on the powertrain, chassis, or tires.

The Bao 5 SUV normally has a towing capacity of over 5,500 lbs (2,500 kg), according to BYD’s Denza brand.

Latest Update: The Overlooked Social Origins of Machiavellian Behavior

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.
  • In 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy.
  • Sources indicate that many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina.

In 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy. While controversial, his magnum opus on statecraft was widely deemed innovative for de-emphasizing ethical norms and ultra-pragmatically explaining what leaders should do to hold and gain power.

Sources indicate that many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature. Like him, they often emerged from ceaselessly unstable, war-prone milieus. Legalists from ancient China viewed Confucians as too morally idealistic; early modern England's Thomas Hobbes held a dimmer view of human nature than did John Locke. Yet, it was the term "Machiavellian" that endured and evolved in English writing since the mid-1500s. Today, it refers to being calculated, insincere, and even unprincipled to gain something.

Recent findings suggest that as a psychological concept, "Machiavellianism" is associated with cynical, manipulative, and self-serving tendencies. Psychologists have even measured it through scales like the MACH-IV and Five-Factor Machiavellianism Inventory. Popular articles and videos abound with titles about how to find "narcissists" among partners, or to beware of "dark triad" traits in co-workers. Whether or not they capture phenomenologically valid constructs, or align with how health professionals use these terms, they do not always include structural approaches and takeaways. Could how Machiavellianism presents in societies give clues into broader social issues needing addressing?

Industry observers note that people with similar childhood adversities can grow up to have very different worldviews. However, for some, a combination of early deprivations, caregiver modeling, and hereditary factors can increase their likelihood of internalizing cynical outlooks. These could crystallize into enduring, Machiavellian patterns of interaction later on. Early childhood attachment disruptions, relational losses, and conditional, inconsistent affection can contribute to understanding relationships as ultimately transactional. Frequent bullying, abuse, or social injustices without accountability might misguide some to view ethical and, sometimes, institutional rules as naive or frivolous.

Later, resulting cravings for "omnipotent control" can lead to great efforts to control how most others view and treat oneself, sometimes in ways contradictory to one's actual self. One applies an astute "theory of mind" for envisioning what others want. Consider a group leader who speaks frequently of uplifting and bringing people together, but privately gossips and plays potential competitors against each other. Or a colleague who cultivates a reputation as a light-hearted jokester, but emotionally abuses their partner at home. Their friends might not believe they have such dissonant traits, let alone have suspected these early on. Indeed, psychoanalysts refer to the superego lacunae of otherwise upstanding people who harbor deeply dark tendencies in specific domains of life.

According to recent reports, but how useful is it, really, to focus on the sensationalism, the individual "wrongness" or "pathology," or the developmental roots of Machiavellian characteristics? Nobody denies that manipulation and relational aggression happen. Individuals with such traits--or at least a strong disposition to them--exist in all human societies, but how and to what extent these manifest depends greatly on one's present and future environments.

Industry observers note that historian E.P. Thompson examined the moral economy of everyday Englishmen in the 1700s, focusing on nuanced motivations of bread riots beyond hunger itself. As Thompson's work supported, people may be at least as driven to drastic action--in his examples, selective intimidation and aggression toward middlemen--by perceived violations of what is normatively reasonable and fair, than by economic inequality in and of itself.

Yet, unlike for his early modern examples, vigilante retribution is no longer as tolerated in most societies. "Fighting fire [i.e. injustices] with fire" can nowadays land people in prison, depending on their methods. Cynicism may then simmer if people see widespread violation of implicit norms of fairness without meaningful consequences.

In a recent development, examples appear painfully difficult for the observer to challenge; they range from deliberate decisions, like leaders' rewarding betrayals of colleagues who find themselves in hard times, to rigidly structural imbalances like co-workers getting overlooked for opportunities due to their ethnicity, gender, or religion. In turn, self-serving, insincere, performative, and manipulative behaviors can become gradually more tolerated, rewarded, and normalized in groups. Generalized trust, authenticity, good-faith charity, and optimism might all slowly wither.

It has been revealed that is it useful to think of widespread Machiavellianism as mutually reinforcing and cyclically associated with greater cynicism in a society? Maybe yes, but that is also not the full picture. Perhaps in most cases, prone to quid pro quo exchanges and transactional alliance-building, Machiavellianism is unlikely to improve social problems long-term. It would not benefit any group's already low-trust culture, declining public confidence in a given institution, or corruption. If anything, the rewarding of one's playing dirty could encourage more of such tendencies in their circles via social learning.

Sources indicate that yet, for some others, witnessing Machiavellianism's normalization might not transform their personalities overall. It would instead outwardly modify their interpersonal approaches to achieving pre-existing, potentially socially constructive goals. These ends, regardless of their means, go beyond everyday self-preservation and range from improving the marginalized social status of one's group to advancing a specific policy.

What might such Machiavellian-like adaptation or imitation look like for someone who did not grow up with overtly congruent traits? Examples include adopting more guardedness and suspicion, calculation and self-restraint in what one indicates and to whom, flattery, selectively concealing one's true feelings, and discreetly discerning colleagues' interests and "agendas." Saying things one does not fully mean or feel may seem advantageous, even encouraged, when one assumes their superiors do the same. One might increasingly rationalize their strategic exploitation of others' misfortunes. If these are the prevailing, implicit rules of engagement in one's organizational or workplace politics, then so they will practice them. As with what Friedrich Nietzsche remarked about fighting monsters, they should also take care lest they essentially "become" Machiavellian through and through.

According to recent reports, not every instance of Machiavellianism in one's workplace, organization, or community indicates a structurally sick society. A few individuals, regardless of how much privilege they have, can still demonstrate such features during periods of widespread optimism and trust, even if their tendencies are more the exception than the norm. Conversely, not everyone who has developed a protective cynicism wants to take advantage of others.

That said, how prevalent Machiavellianism is in a group at a given time may hint at underlying competition over resources perceived as both finite and unfairly allocated. Resources are not necessarily just material wealth, but also social capital, status, and power. Underhanded ways of interaction may reflect not just neurodevelopmental predispositions but also, for those who are most angry, disillusioned, or hardened, an instrumental means of efficiently accumulating such resources.

Industry observers note that none of this absolves the need for accountability and responsibility for inflicting interpersonal harms. Advocacy can be done primarily through good-faith methods. Leaders can promote workplace cultures that are more fair and transparent than what they knew in the past. Yet, so long as racism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia, and other social ills persist, Machiavellianism may continue to appear to some a legitimate way of navigating work and life--not just for those seeking to maintain great privilege, but also, and perhaps especially, for many people without much of it.

Industry News: Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table.
  • It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert.
  • Industry observers note that for generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table. The flesh has been cooked until soft. But the hard part is still ahead. To turn the pumpkin into pie, the cook must mash it, scrape it, and force it through a sieve, separating smooth pulp from stubborn strings and fibers. There is no can of pumpkin puree. No food processor. Just the pumpkin, rudimentary kitchen tools, and a lot of elbow grease. The work could take hours, all for an eight-person dessert. An 1876 New England cookbook, for example, instructed cooks to simmer pumpkin for six to eight hours, stirring frequently, before rubbing it through a colander.

It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert. Pumpkin flesh doesn’t naturally break down into a silky puree. Cooking softens its tissues, but turning the squash into smooth filling requires additional mechanical work.

Industry observers note that for generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle. Eventually, factories took over the work of cooking and processing pumpkins into puree. But the solution didn’t stop there. Growers also turned to pumpkin varieties with naturally smoother, less fibrous flesh, making the job easier before the squash even reached the factory.

According to recent reports, pumpkin was an crucial food in North America long before Thanksgiving became a national holiday. Indigenous peoples cultivated and prepared the squash in many forms, and European colonists adopted pumpkins as a plentiful crop. Colonists adapted their own pie-making traditions to the abundant squash, incorporating pumpkin into sweet and savory pies. By the 17th century, recipes for pumpkin-filled pies were appearing in English cookbooks.

According to recent reports, in 1796, the first known American cookbook, Amelia Simmons’s American Cookery, included a recipe for “Pompkin Pudding” made with cooked pumpkin, milk, eggs, and spices. Before the pumpkin could be combined with the other ingredients, the recipe called for it to be strained, separating fine pulp from tougher material.

Thanksgiving didn’t take shape as a national tradition until the mid-19th century. Pumpkins were harvested in the fall and could be stored through the colder months, making them a natural ingredient for a holiday associated with the autumn harvest.

It has been revealed that the story of the Pilgrims sitting down with Native Americans for the first Thanksgiving has some truth to it, too. In 1621, English colonists and members of the Wampanoag people did gather for a three-day harvest celebration. But the friendly, feel-good version passed down in schoolbooks leaves out a much more complicated history of colonialism and conflict.

It wasn’t until over two centuries later that Sarah Josepha Hale, a prominent magazine editor, campaigned for decades for a national holiday, and, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “day of Thanksgiving.” She believed a shared day of gratitude, centered on family and community, could help unite a country increasingly divided by political conflict.

Hale also helped popularize the foods associated with the holiday, promoting a traditional Latest England Thanksgiving menu through her magazine. Pumpkin pie was already a regional favorite, but as Thanksgiving spread nationally after the Civil War, the dessert became part of the broader American tradition.

Pumpkin pie became increasingly associated with the holiday meal during this era, drawing on its roots in Newly introduced England’s seasonal cooking traditions. Preparing it remained labor-intensive, and results varied.

Industry observers note that industrial food processing offered a solution to the labor-intensive process of making pumpkin pie. Factories could cook and mechanically break down pumpkin in large quantities, producing puree without requiring every household to repeat the tedious process. Canning transformed pumpkin from a seasonal ingredient demanding considerable preparation into a convenient product that could be stored and used when needed.

John Coupland, Ph.D., professor of food science at Penn State, describes the work involved in preparing pumpkin by hand as “astonishing.” Industrial processing made pie filling far more convenient, eliminating the need to cook, mash, and strain a pumpkin from scratch.

It also gave bakers a reliable starting point, helping make pumpkin pie more consistent and cementing its place at the Thanksgiving table.

Sources indicate that making pumpkin puree is more complicated than simply cooking the flesh until soft. Pumpkin cells are surrounded by walls containing materials such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cooking softens the tissue, while mechanical processing breaks it into smaller particles. Together, these processes help determine the puree’s texture and moisture.

According to recent reports, the goal is a smooth puree that is neither watery nor full of tough fibers. The pumpkin variety matters, as do the heating conditions and mechanical methods used to break down its flesh.

Modern food processing allows manufacturers to control these variables on a large scale, producing batches with similar textures and moisture levels. That predictability is especially valuable in pumpkin pie, where the filling’s consistency helps determine the finished dessert.

But the food industry found another way to improve the process: start with a pumpkin better suited to the job.

That is where Libby’s, one of the country’s largest canned-pumpkin producers, and the Dickinson pumpkin enter the story.

According to Libby’s, farmer Elijah Dickinson brought special Dickinson pumpkin seeds from Kentucky to Illinois in 1835. The variety became closely associated with commercial pumpkin processing, and Libby, McNeill & Libby acquired Dickinson & Co. in 1929, strengthening the company’s connection to the crop.

Industry observers note that dickinson pumpkins look different from the bright orange pumpkins sold for carving (often called field pumpkins). Their tan skin matters less to processors than the dense flesh beneath it. Relatively high in solids and sugars, Dickinson pumpkins are particularly well-suited to puree.

Many carving pumpkins, by contrast, have stringier flesh that makes them harder to process into a smooth puree. Coupland explains that they are not ideally suited to commercial food production because their fibers can be difficult to break down.

In a recent development, coupland describes Dickinson puree as having a “smooth, even texture,” adding that it means you won’t be “picking fibers out of your teeth.” Rather than trying to eliminate the stringiness of a carving pumpkin, processors can start with a variety whose natural characteristics make the job easier. The raw material itself becomes part of the technology.

Libby’s helped bring this approach into American kitchens through its canned-pumpkin business, pairing a suitable variety with industrial processing to deliver consistent puree to home bakers.

Interestingly, Dickinson pumpkins belong to Cucurbita moschata, a species that includes several varieties of winter squash. Many familiar carving pumpkins belong to Cucurbita pepo. Botanically, the distinction between pumpkin and squash is largely a matter of common usage rather than a strict scientific boundary. The FDA permits certain sweet, golden-fleshed squashes to be labeled as pumpkin in canned products, reflecting the longstanding overlap in how the terms are used in the food trade.

For pumpkin pie, what matters most is the flesh inside: how it tastes, how it breaks down, and how consistently it performs. Today’s Thanksgiving cooks no longer needs to work themselves to the bone because the food industry has learned to do the work first.

Tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.

It has been revealed that that’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.

Tesla Charging declared the new station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:.

Upcoming Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb.

Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.

It has been revealed that texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February, Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”.

The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.

Tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, confirmed high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.

Here’s every public Megacharger currently live on Tesla’s map:.

It has been revealed that that’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October, there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.

So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.

Tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.

Industry observers note that tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report indicated about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has stated Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

To hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.

Sources indicate that pilot said in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very big one.

Sources indicate that and the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla launched volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it stated last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Big fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, noted Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

Sources indicate that “By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she noted.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Industry observers note that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he remarked. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

It has been revealed that A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy noted.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

Recent findings suggest that by age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

According to recent reports, wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Sources indicate that the study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

According to recent reports, cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive initiative,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.
